blocks: Animal cruelty is a broad term used to describe criminal offences committed against animals. Much like crimes against humans, these offences range in severity, type, cognisability and scale. It is important to note that animals are the victims in these cases, and must be treated as such. There are a number of different legal provisions enacted for the protection of animals in the country. This Handbook is to serve as a ready reference to these statutory provisions protecting animals, and the procedure to be followed in such scenarios, for the ease of filing complaints and conducting investigations in cases involving crimes against animals.

It is important to note that the definition of “animal” as per the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act, 1960 is any living creature that is not human. This is a wide definition meant to include all animals within the protection of the law. Further, the term “owner” refers not just to the true owner, but also any person having possession or custody of an animal, with or without the consent of the true owner. Therefore, any person who has an animal in their care is legally considered to be the owner, and consequently, responsible for the wellbeing of the animal.

Chapter II lays down the specific legal procedures to be followed when handling cases involving crimes against animals. Chapters III-XI provide an overview of the different types of criminal offences against animals, and the relevant legal provisions, and Chapter XII provides state-specific statutory provisions.
Legal Procedure Upon Receipt of Animal Cruelty Complaints

Cruelty to animals is a criminal offence, therefore the provisions of the Bhartiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS), the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA), and the procedures prescribed in The Prevention of Cruelty to Animals (Care and Maintenance of Case Property Animals) Rules, 2017 (“Case Property Rules”) along with the Bhartiya Nagrik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) shall apply. In addition, specific legislation, i.e. The Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act, 1960 (“PCA”) and allied Rules are also applicable. Further, since these offences are vetero-legal cases, they require specific procedures to be followed (similar to medico-legal cases).

Upon receipt of information about the commission of a cognizable offence, it is the duty of the police officer in charge of a police station to register an FIR under section 173(1), BNSS. [Hon’ble Supreme Court in Lalita Kumari v. Government of Uttar Pradesh and Others, 2014(2)SCC 1]
Information is receivable orally, which shall be reduced in writing by the office incharge of the police station or by electronic communication [Section 173(1)(i) & (ii) BNSS].
Upon information of cognizable offence, FIR shall be registered at any police station, regardless of the place of occurrence of offence. [Section 173(1), BNSS].
FIR shall also be registered when such information is received electronically, with the informant's signature required within three days [Section 173(1)(ii), BNSS],
A copy of the recorded information shall be given to the informant or victim immediately and free of cost. [Section 173(2), BNSS]

For cognizable offences punishable by three to seven years, the officer in charge may, with prior permission from an officer of the rank of Deputy Superintendent of Police or above, conduct a preliminary enquiry within 14 days to ascertain if there's a prima facie case, or proceed with investigation if a prima facie case exists. [Section 173(3), BNSS]

If an officer refuses to record the information, the aggrieved person can send the information in writing to the Superintendent of Police. If the Superintendent finds that the information discloses a cognizable offence, they must investigate or direct an investigation. [Section 173(4), BNSS].

Every police officer also has the duty to prevent the commission of cognizable offences, to the best of their ability [Section 168, BNSS], which includes informing their superior officers [Section 169, BNSS], and arresting a suspect,
A copy of the recorded information shall be given to the informant or victim immediately and free of cost. [Section 173(2), BNSS]

For cognizable offences punishable by three to seven years, the officer in charge may, with prior permission from an officer of the rank of Deputy Superintendent of Police or above, conduct a preliminary enquiry within 14 days to ascertain if there's a prima facie case, or proceed with investigation if a prima facie case exists. [Section 173(3), BNSS]

If an officer refuses to record the information, the aggrieved person can send the information in writing to the Superintendent of Police. If the Superintendent finds that the information discloses a cognizable offence, they must investigate or direct an investigation. [Section 173(4), BNSS].

Every police officer also has the duty to prevent the commission of cognizable offences, to the best of their ability [Section 168, BNSS], which includes informing their superior officers [Section 169, BNSS], and arresting a suspect, without orders from a Magistrate and without a warrant, if the situation so requires. [Section 170(1), BNSS], provided that the person so arrested is not detained for a period exceeding 24 hours from the time of arrest, unless further detention is required or authorised under any law at the time being in force.

When informed about the commission of a non-cognizable offence, the police officer in charge of a police station must ensure that details of the offence are entered in a book prescribed in a form as prescribed by the state government. [Section 174(1), BNSS].
The officer must also refer such information to the Magistrate [Section 174(1)(i), BNSS] and forward the daily diary report of all such cases fortnightly to the Magistrate [Section 174(1)(ii), BNSS]
Note: If a case involves both cognizable and non-cognizable offences, it shall be deemed a cognizable case [Section 174(4), BNSS].

A non-cognizable offence can only be investigated upon the order of a Magistrate [Section 174(2), BNSS]. Once such order is received, the investigation will proceed in the same manner as that of a cognizable offence, except the power to arrest without warrant. [Section 174(3), BNSS ].

However, any police officer in charge of a police station has the power to investigate any cognizable offence within their station's jurisdiction, without requiring an order from a Magistrate [Section 175, BNSS]. A copy of the report of the cognizable offence must be sent to the Magistrate to keep them informed of the status of the investigation [Section 176(1), BNSS].

The Magistrate may order an investigation on private complaints after making an enquiry on the complaint or considering submissions made by the police officer regarding the complaint. [Section 175(3) of BNSS]

Magistrate may order investigation against public servants, subject to receiving a report from the officer superior to the concerned public servant and considering assertions made by the public servant about the alleged incident.[Section 175(4), BNSS].

The investigating officer is required to maintain a daily record of the investigation in a case diary, and include all details such as the statements recorded, places visited, facts ascertained, etc. [Section 192, BNSS].

While conducting an investigation, a police officer also has the power to require the attendance of any person who appears to be acquainted with the facts and circumstances of the case, and resides within the jurisdiction of that or adjoining station’s jurisdiction [Section 179, BNSS]. They are also empowered to orally examine witnesses and record their statement in writing [Section 180(1), BNSS].

Officers are empowered to conduct searches during the course of the investigation [Section 185, BNSS]. The search must be conducted by the officer in person, if practicable [Section 185(2), BNSS] and recorded through audio-video electronic means, preferably by mobile phone [Proviso to Section 185(2), BNSS]. Copies of any record made must be sent to the nearest empowered Magistrate within 48 hours.[Section 185(5), BNSS].
Police officers not below the rank of sub-Inspector also have the powers of search and seizure for offences under the PCA Act [Sections 32 and 34, PCA Act].
Searches relating to an offence under the PCA Act that has been, is being or is about to be committed, can be undertaken upon the issuance of a search warrant from a Magistrate [Section 33, PCA Act].

Any police officer above the rank of constable also has a general power to seize an animal if they have reason to believe that an offence against this Act has been, is being or is about to be committed against the animal, and produce the same for examination to the jurisdictional veterinary officer [Section 34, PCA Act].

Upon seizure of an animal, the seizing authority shall ensure health inspection, identification, and marking through the jurisdictional veterinary officer and produce the same before the Magistrate [Rule 3, Case Property Rules].

Any other article of evidentiary value such as a weapon (knife/rod/hammer/stone/gun/stick, etc.), heavy chains, cage in which animal was confined, or any other relevant matter must be taken into custody as well and produced before the magistrate, along with photographs, health/forensic reports and statements [Section 106, BNSS].

Electronic records, such as videos, CCTV camera footage, photographs, etc. are deemed to be documents, and must also be included as evidence [Section 63 of BSA.]. If the electronic record is of the nature that cannot be produced in court, a certificate attesting to the evidence, device it was recorded on, circumstances of such recording, etc., and signed by the person who operates said device, must also be issued [Section 63(4) of BSA].
Any vehicle used in the commission of an offence under the PCA Act must be seized and produced before the magistrate for directions to hold it as security [Rule 5(4), Case Property Rules].
Standard Operating Procedures: When the animal is alive

When a police officer is made aware of a situation where an animal has been or is being abused, and the animal is alive, they must go to the location and conduct a search [authorised under section 32, 34 PCA Act], and the animal in question must be seized [authorised under section 34, PCA Act].

The police officer must next contact the Jurisdictional Veterinary Officer to arrange for identification tagging in the manner prescribed [Rule 3, Case Property Rules], and a medical examination of the animal. [See Annexure-A for a sample letter to the Jurisdictional Veterinary Officer]
In case the animal has sustained any injuries or is sick, they must be given the necessary medical treatment [Section 35, PCA Act].

The animal must be produced before the Magistrate, who will decide upon the custody of the animal pending litigation. Cost of care and maintenance of the animal is to be borne by the accused, who must pay the bond within 3 days, failing which the animal shall be forfeited. The seized animal is then to be shifted to the infirmary/pinjrapole/SPCA/Animal Welfare Organisation that has been granted custody. [Rules 3-5, Case Property Rules].

The animal against which an offense under the PCA Act is committed/alleged to have been committed cannot be returned to the accused while the trial is pending. [Hon’ble Supreme Court in State of UP v. Mustakeem & Ors., Criminal Appeal Nos. 283-287/2002].

When the animal is alive but mortally wounded/diseased

When a police officer is made aware of a situation where an animal has been or is If a police officer above the rank of constable comes across an animal who is severely injured or diseased, they must contact the Jurisdictional Veterinary Officer to arrange for the medical examination of the animal. [See Annexure-A for a sample letter to the District Veterinary Officer]
If the veterinary officer certifies that keeping the animal alive would cause unnecessary suffering, the animal can be euthanized after obtaining consent from the Magistrate [Section 13, PCA Act].

If the animal victim is already dead, the police officer must contact the Jurisdictional Veterinary Officer to arrange for a postmortem examination of the animal. [See Annexure-A for a sample letter to the Jurisdictional Veterinary Officer]

The body must immediately be seized and sent to the Jurisdictional Veterinary Officer for post-mortem examination. In cases of suspected poisoning, viscera must be sent to a forensic laboratory once the veterinarian has sealed and stamped the sample.
The post-mortem report received from the Jurisdictional Veterinary Officer, identifying the cause of death, must be included with the investigation report, and in the case diary.
The carcass of the animal can be duly disposed of after the post mortem examination.
When drugs and injurious substances are found

Situations where drugs and injurious substances may be present require a similar operating procedure as that of handling illegal drugs. When drugs or injurious substances are found during a search, they must be seized and sent to the designated laboratory.
When a Drug Inspector is a part of the search, the seized substances must be sealed by the Drug Inspector and sent to the designated laboratory.
The completion of the investigation should be carried out without unnecessary delay. [Section 193(1), BNSS].
Upon completion of the investigation, the police report must be submitted to the empowered Magistrate [Section 193(3), BNSS].
The informant or victim should be informed about the progress of the investigation within 90 days [Section 193(3)(ii) of the BNSS].
Further investigation is permitted even after the submission of the police report to the Magistrate [Section 193(9), BNSS].

If further investigation is required during the trial, it necessitates permission from the Court and must be completed within 90 days, extensible with Court permission.[Proviso to Section 193(9), BNSS]
